lead: A real pipe never has only straight pipe. Water enters from a tank, passes elbows and valves, and leaves into another tank. Friction along the straight length causes the major loss. Each fitting causes a local disturbance and a minor loss. Engineers add both to get the total head the pump must supply. The same numbers decide pump size, pipe diameter and whether a short suction line will cavitate. This chapter gives the Darcy-Weisbach major loss, the K-coefficient minor loss, and the total-loss rule.
prereq: You need the Darcy-Weisbach equation from 4.3 and the Bernoulli equation from Unit 3.

blocks.text: The Darcy-Weisbach equation gives the loss in a straight constant-diameter pipe. It is the major loss because a long line has far more straight pipe than fittings. Loss is a head in metres of the flowing fluid.

blocks.where: h<sub>f</sub> is friction head loss in m; f is the Darcy friction factor, dimensionless; L is straight pipe length in m; D is internal diameter in m; V is mean velocity in m/s; g = 9.81 m/s².

blocks.text: A fitting turns or changes the flow area. Extra turbulence converts mechanical energy into heat. This local loss is the minor loss. Its coefficient K is dimensionless and depends on fitting shape and, weakly, on Reynolds number.

blocks.where: h<sub>m</sub> is minor head loss in m; K is the fitting loss coefficient, dimensionless; V is the local mean velocity in m/s; g = 9.81 m/s².

blocks.text: Add all losses for the system. Use the velocity of each segment; use one velocity only when the diameter is the same. Total head loss is the sum of major and minor losses.
H<sub>L</sub> = Σ [f L V²/(2gD)] + Σ [K V²/(2g)]
blocks.where: H<sub>L</sub> is total head loss in m; the first sum covers straight segments; the second covers fittings; each term uses the local V and D.

blocks.text: Handbooks list K for standard fittings. Values below are typical for turbulent water flow; use manufacturer data for design. Exit loss is exactly one velocity head because all kinetic energy is lost in the receiving tank.

A sudden expansion has a standard result from momentum balance: h<sub>ex</sub> = (V<sub>1</sub> − V<sub>2</sub>)²/(2g), where V<sub>1</sub> is the mean velocity in the smaller upstream pipe in m/s, V<sub>2</sub> is the mean velocity in the larger downstream pipe in m/s, and h<sub>ex</sub> is expansion head loss in m. For a sudden contraction, K is based on the downstream velocity and is about 0.5 for a sharp edge.

Equivalent length converts a fitting into straight pipe of the same loss. Set K V²/(2g) = f (L<sub>e</sub>/D) V²/(2g), so L<sub>e</sub> = K D/f. Here L<sub>e</sub> is equivalent length in m, D is pipe diameter in m, f is the Darcy friction factor and K is the fitting coefficient. A valve with K = 2.5 in a 50 mm pipe with f = 0.03 adds L<sub>e</sub> = 2.5 × 0.05/0.03 = 4.17 m.

A long pipe has large L/D. Major loss grows with L/D, while minor loss stays a fixed number of velocity heads. Minor losses can be dropped when ΣK is small compared with fL/D. With typical ΣK of 5–10 and f ≈ 0.02–0.03, L/D must be a few thousand before minor losses drop below 10% of the major loss. For a short pipe, pump suction, manifold or laboratory rig, fittings can dominate. Never drop minor losses just because the word 'minor' appears.

items: Draw the line from start tank to end tank and number every straight run and fitting.
Find diameter, length and mean velocity in each run.
Find f from the Moody diagram using Reynolds number and relative roughness (see 4.4).
Add K for every fitting; use the local velocity for each.
Add major and minor losses. The pump head must cover this total plus any lift and pressure difference.

blocks.text: The total energy line falls by each loss; the hydraulic gradient line sits one velocity head below it. See 4.6 for the drawing.

examples.question: A 50 mm diameter pipe is 20 m long and carries water at a mean velocity of 1.2 m/s. The Darcy friction factor is 0.03. The line has a sharp entrance (K = 0.5), two 90° elbows (K = 0.9 each), one valve (K = 2.5) and an exit into a tank (K = 1.0). Find the velocity head, major loss, minor loss, total head loss and the equivalent length of all fittings. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
steps: Sum K: entrance 0.5 + two elbows 2 × 0.9 = 1.8 + valve 2.5 + exit 1.0 gives ΣK = 5.8.
Total head loss: H_L = h_f + h_m = 0.8807 + 0.4257 = 1.3064 m, about 1.306 m.
Equivalent length: L_e = ΣK D/f = 5.8 × 0.05/0.03 = 9.667 m.
examples.answer: The total head loss is 1.306 m of water; the fittings are equivalent to 9.667 m of the same pipe.
examples.check:
def main():
    g = 9.81
    D = 0.05
    L = 20.0
    V = 1.2
    f = 0.03
    Ksum = 0.5 + 2*0.9 + 2.5 + 1.0
    hv = V**2/(2*g)
    major = f*L/D*hv
    minor = Ksum*hv
    total = major + minor
    Le = Ksum*D/f
    print(f'{hv:.4f}')
    print(f'{major:.3f}')
    print(f'{minor:.3f}')
    print(f'{total:.3f}')
    print(f'{Le:.3f}')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

traps: Using one velocity head for all fittings when diameters change. Each K must multiply the local V²/(2g).
Adding K values for a sudden expansion. Use h = (V₁ − V₂)²/(2g) with the two pipe velocities.
Thinking minor losses are always small. In a short pipe or pump suction, ΣK can exceed fL/D.
Using mm for D in fL/D or in L_e = KD/f. Convert D to metres first: 50 mm is 0.05 m, so 20/0.05 = 400 and 5.8 × 0.05/0.03 = 9.667 m.
Mixing head loss in metres with pressure drop in Pa. Multiply head by ρg when pump data is in pressure.

quiz.q: State the Darcy-Weisbach major-loss formula and define f, L, D and V.
quiz.a: h_f = f(L/D)V²/(2g); f is the Darcy friction factor, L pipe length, D diameter, V mean velocity.

quiz.q: Why is the exit loss coefficient K = 1.0 for a pipe discharging into a large tank?
quiz.a: All kinetic energy V²/(2g) is dissipated in the tank; the tank velocity is nearly zero, so the loss equals one velocity head.

quiz.q: Water flows at 2 m/s through two fittings, each K = 0.75. Find the minor loss. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
A 100 m long, 100 mm pipe has f = 0.02, V = 1 m/s and ΣK = 4. Compare major and minor loss. Can minor loss be ignored?
quiz.a: Velocity head = 1/19.62 = 0.0510 m. Major = 0.02 × (100/0.1) × 0.0510 = 1.019 m. Minor = 4 × 0.0510 = 0.204 m. Minor is about 20% of the major loss, and about 17% of the total loss (0.204 + 1.019 = 1.223 m). It is not negligible for an accurate answer.

quiz.q: A sudden expansion from 50 mm to 100 mm carries 5 L/s of water. Find the expansion loss. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
Why does a globe valve have a much larger K than a fully open gate valve?
quiz.a: A globe valve forces flow through a winding passage with large turning and restriction; an open gate valve leaves a nearly clear bore.

quiz.q: Give the equivalent-length formula for a fitting and state one use.
quiz.a: L_e = K D/f; it converts a minor loss into the length of straight pipe that gives the same loss, so fittings and pipe can be compared directly.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, pipe-network software stores K values for thousands of fittings and solves the whole network with friction and minor losses together. Pump suction lines are sized with extra care because a large K close to the pump lowers local pressure and can cause cavitation; see Unit 7, NPSH. Search for 'minor loss coefficients' and 'pipe network analysis' to go deeper. District water systems and building services use these ideas every day.
